title: Brioche stole
subtitle: A rectangular DK stole in two-colour brioche stitch — warm, reversible, and squishy.
excerpt: A rectangular stole in DK wool worked in two-colour brioche stitch throughout. Both colours are worked on the same needle simultaneously, creating a reversible fabric where each side shows one dominant colour. Finished size approximately 35 cm wide by 175 cm long, blocked. About 200 g each of two DK yarns in contrasting values.
sourceNotes: Two-colour brioche stitch is documented in Nancy Marchant, Brioche Knitting (2010), Chapter 1: Two-colour brioche basics. The technique is well established; the two-colour brioche stitch itself predates Marchant's formalization and appears in various craft references from the 1940s onward. This pattern uses the standard brk/brp brioche notation.

glossaryTerms.definition: Knit together the next stitch and its yarn-over from the previous row. In two-colour brioche, brk is worked on the colour that was not worked on the previous pass.
Purl together the next stitch and its yarn-over from the previous row. Worked on the colour that was not worked on the previous pass.
Slip the next stitch purlwise with the yarn over the needle. This creates the paired stitch that will be worked as a brk or brp on the following pass.

content.text: A rectangular stole in DK wool worked in two-colour brioche stitch, with each side of the fabric showing one dominant colour in a deep, squishy rib. Finished size approximately 35 × 175 cm. The fabric is fully reversible and does not require blocking.

Two-colour brioche works two passes per row: a setup pass and a work pass. The two yarns alternate on each pass and are never worked on the same pass, so the colour management is straightforward once the pattern is established. Budget about 200 g (about 440 m / 480 yards) of each of two DK yarns in strongly contrasting values (light and dark work best). The needle size is slightly larger than for standard DK to account for the fabric's natural compression.

content.text: 20 stitches and 28 rows to 10 cm over two-colour brioche stitch on 4.5 mm needles, relaxed. Two-colour brioche is not blocked (wet blocking would flatten the rib structure irreversibly). Measure the gauge swatch relaxed after washing. If your swatch runs wider than gauge, the stole will be wider than 35 cm; at 18 stitches per 10 cm it will be approximately 39 cm.

content.text: Using colour A and the long-tail cast-on, cast on 70 stitches (odd number if adjusted). Cast-on tail: allow approximately 55 cm for a 70-stitch long-tail.
, k1; repeat from * to end. Turn.
Row 1 (colour B, WS): sl1yo, *brp, sl1yo; repeat from * to last st, brp.
Row 2 (colour A, RS): brk, *sl1yo, brk; repeat from * to last st, sl1yo.

Repeat rows 1 and 2, alternating colours on each row, until the stole measures 175 cm from cast-on edge, ending with a row 2. The stole grows approximately 7 rows per 2.5 cm at gauge; the 175 cm length requires approximately 490 rows total.

Standard bind-off in brioche pattern (each brk or sl1yo is worked as its matching brk/sl1yo before being bound off). Work loosely. The brioche bind-off should match the cast-on edge in stretch and appearance.
Every 50 rows (approximately 18 cm): the stitch count on the needle must remain 70 throughout. In brioche each row only works half the stitches; the remaining stitches are carried as sl1yo pairs.

Working both colours on the same pass: this creates a non-brioche fabric without the paired rib structure. Each pass must use only one colour: colour A on even rows, colour B on odd rows. If the two yarns are at the same end of the needle, a colour has been worked twice in a row.
Dropped yarn-over from sl1yo: the brioche stitch on the following pass looks like a regular stitch with no paired yo. The next

must knit or purl 2 together; if the yo is missing, there is only 1 stitch, which cannot be worked as a brioche stitch. Pick up the dropped yo loop from the previous row and place it back on the needle before the orphaned stitch.

Brioche stole is not wet-blocked. Hand wash gently, roll in a towel to remove excess water, and lay flat to dry. The rib structure recovers naturally as it dries. Do not pin out the width, as the rib draw-in is part of the design.
Hand wash in cool water, lay flat to dry. The two-colour brioche fabric is naturally elastic and recovers well after washing.
Try a two-colour brioche triangle shawl. Use the same brioche pattern in each wing with top-down triangle shaping, increasing every RS row. Both colours alternate on each pass as before.
